title: What Learning Looks Like in Action - 4
author: Martin Skelton
summary: In this installment Skelton describes the third visible state of learning, treading water, using his own history as a principal who proudly showed parents silent, busy classrooms. He argues that smooth, fast, correct work is a sign that learning has already happened, not that it is happening. Real learning appears as struggle, so looking for it means looking for hesitation and effort rather than fluency. He distinguishes accomplishment from learning and warns against judging school performances as if they were finished products. He nonetheless allows that a little treading water can be valuable, for enjoyment, for recovery when tired, for protecting focus when two learning goals might clash, and at assessment time. The central test is whether students are busy or busy learning.
points: Silent, busy, correct work often shows that learning is already finished rather than under way.
Because learning happens in the gap between where a learner is and where they want to be, evidence of learning is evidence of good struggle.
Skelton separates accomplishment from learning and says school performances should be read as getting better in action, not judged as polished finals.
Treading water is acceptable in small doses for pleasure, recovery, focus on one goal at a time, and assessment, but too much wastes time and teaches that performing beats improving.
quotes: Learning doesn’t happen when everything is already sticky. It happens when it isn’t. Learning happens when things don’t go smoothly, often obviously so during new learning and, slowly, less obviously so during consolidating learning. By the time things are going smoothly, the learning is, for now, already over.

The reason that the students in those classes in my school to which I eagerly took parents were furiously and apparently successfully writing in their exercise books was, of course, precisely because they weren't struggling. They could already do everything they were being asked to. Their speed at completing the work appropriately and with little hesitation was precisely a measure of the fact that, when we visited, no learning was happening; it had already happened sometime before.

Learning is the process of moving from where I am to somewhere I want to get to. The gap between the two is where my learning happens. Whilst I am learning, you won’t see accomplishment (except of the things that are already sticky); you’ll see a good struggle.

Too much treading water is not a good thing. It wastes student time, it eats into the extended time that good struggling needs, and it helps students and teachers learn that performing is more important than getting things better.
Learning takes energy, huge amounts of energy. When we don’t have any energy left, treading water is the wonderful harbour we go to for safety.

Finally, of course, treading water is where we hope our students to be when it comes to assessment time. We don’t want assessment to be a struggle, we want its to be a performance of what has already been learned. If our students are having to struggle by the time they reach their assessment, either something has gone wrong in their previous learning or the assessment is not actually assessing what it should be.
In the end, though, schools are places where children and students (and teachers and Principals) are supposed to get better. It’s what schools exist for.
